ety.text: From Middle French pause, from Latin pausa, from Ancient Greek παῦσις (paûsis), from Ancient Greek παύω (paúō, “stop”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of pausa.

senses.d: To take a temporary rest, take a break for a short period after an effort.
To stop (an activity) for a while.
To interrupt an activity and wait.
ex: When telling the scary story, he paused for effect.
Tarry, pause a day or two.

senses.d: To hesitate; to hold back; to delay.
ex: Why doth the Jew pause? Take thy forfeiture.

senses.d: To halt the play or playback of, temporarily, so that it can be resumed from the same point.
ex: to pause a song, a video, or a computer game
Press Start at any time to pause the game.

senses.d: A temporary stop or rest; an intermission of action; interruption; suspension; cessation.
A short time for relaxing and doing something else.
In writing and printing, a mark indicating the place and nature of an arrest of voice in reading; a punctuation mark.
ex: Teach the pupil to mind the pauses.

senses.d: A break or paragraph in writing.
A sign indicating continuance of a note or rest.
Used immediately after a statement to indicate that there was no innuendo or homosexual meaning intended, especially when such a meaning is a reasonable interpretation.

grp.label: to take a temporary rest or break

es:descansar.gl: to rest, relax (be in a state of rest or inactivity)

ety.text: From Middle French interrompre, partial relatinization of Old French entrerompre, itself a calque of Latin interrumpere.
Borrowed from Latin pausāre. Compare the inherited doublet posar. Cognate with English pause.
